Recent photometric surveys of the Trans-Neptunian Objects zone have revealed a distinct bimodal distribution among these objects.  The majority of these objects exhibit dark colors, classified as r - I > 0.4, whereas a smaller subgroup displays brighter colors, typically exceeding r - I < 0.2.  Notably, a portion of these objects have colors that fall in between these two extremes with r - I ranging from -0.4 to 0.4.  Research has suggested that these objects with moderate colors exhibit signs of recent reprocessing, whereas observations of the objects' spectra do not indicate significant changes.  Observations of two objects, 2007 EU182 and 2003 AZ84, suggest that their surfaces are composed of a mixture of fresh and processed materials with the ratio of these components varying over time due to the random emergence of the surface features.  As a result, these objects appear to have colors that fluctuate over time.  As a result of the same phenomenon, it is likely that the objects with moderate colors are in fact part of the group of objects with the dark colors.  As a result, it is likely that the bimodal distribution observed in the objects' colors is a result of the objects' colors fluctuating over time.

The mechanical properties of a specific alloy, Ti-6Al, were studied using a combination of experimental and simulated methods. A new mathematical model based on a rate-dependent flow rule was developed to describe the behavior of this alloy in its initial stages. This model was effective in replicating the stress response of this alloy as it undergoes various strain rates and temperatures. Additionally, the model accurately predicted the internal stress buildup in this alloy when tested under different conditions. The simulation results showed that the alloy exhibits distinct deformation stages, including slip and creep, which were also observed in the experimental data. The model successfully identified the threshold stresses required for these stages to occur at different temperatures, providing valuable insights into the alloy's mechanical properties.

Software Product Lines, or SPLs, enable the development of adaptable systems by allowing a single codebase to be tailored to meet the needs of various distinct product variants through the integration of Feature Models. However, maintaining Feature Models can be complex, particularly when they undergo changes. Consequently, it is crucial to validate these models to guarantee they can be correctly processed by the underlying system. This research aims to develop a validation tool for SPL Feature Models, built on the concept of constraint trees, which can be manipulated to validate the correctness of the models. The tool allows users to define constraints, either globally or locally, in the form of a constraint tree that must be satisfied by the SPL Feature Model. Users can leverage the tool to check for the presence or absence of certain conditions within the SPL Feature Model, such as the absence of cross-violations between variant configurations.

A newly developed Python package, called PyCSP, has been created for generating synthetic images and deep point spread profile (PSF) profiles, used for testing and training high-contrast imaging data reduction algorithms. The package, available at https://github.com/AdelleG/PyCSP, can generate thousands of PSFs per second, utilizing a GPU and thus significantly faster than previous software. The algorithm relies on ray tracing to generate accurate PSFs, and our results demonstrate the package's efficiency and accuracy. The results show that PyCSP can reach completion rates of up to 1000 times faster than commercial GPUs for generating hundreds of PSFs. Our testing with various PSF models, including those with known properties, showed that PyCSP can achieve sub-nanometer accuracy under ideal conditions. We demonstrate the capabilities of PyCSP by generating 10,000 PSFs, which were then used to train an artificial neural network for detecting faint companions in astrometry tasks.

We examine the features of symmetry-resolved entropies during the black hole evaporation process, which is influenced by the remaining black hole and its charged or spin properties. Our investigation is performed using various models that take into account the black hole's remaining parameters, which are derived from generalizations of the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy formula. We apply this framework to study not only black holes in a de Sitter universe but also those in a fixed background, where the latter case is extended to include charges. Our analysis of the black hole's final stages provides insights into the fine structure of the black hole and its connection to the remaining parameters.

In the case of Fermi arcs in Weyl semimetals, our research delves into how surface states interact with each other when there are multiple Weyl nodes present. We investigate the outcome of these interactions by analyzing the underlying physics, using a non-Fermi liquid model to support our findings. We find that the surface states split and form distinct bands, with each band exhibiting power-law behavior on the surface along with a corresponding in the bulk, resulting in a net zero total Berry curvature across the entire system. This research also extends to examining how Fermi arcs in topological insulators with higher-order Dirac cones transition into this new state as anisotropy decreases.

We present an innovative training approach grounded in the principles of data augmentation accessibility. The method's effectiveness is evident in the straightforward implementation, minimal need for hyperparameter fine-tuning, and the ability to enhance the performance of any pre-existing video prediction model. In our experiments, this technique enhanced the performance of the World Model and LSTM models on the DeepMind Lab environment by 30% and increased the diversity of its predictions. Furthermore, this method was successfully applied to other models, including Deep Stack GAN, Deep Recurrent GAN, and the Implicit Maximum Likelihood Estimation model, achieving state-of-the-art results of 3.79, 3.94, and 3.75 average L2 error respectively after only a limited number of training frames.

Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations are frequently associated with aging
processes. As a typical mtDNA contains 16,569 base pairs, various mutations
have been discovered, and many more are anticipated to be identified. These
mutations can arise in specific individuals or across diverse species. A
mathematical framework is provided to analyze the co-evolution of mtDNA
mutations within a population. The resulting dynamics are contingent upon the
particular path of the main species population and are influenced by the level
of species overlap and the rate of mitochondrial transfer between organisms.
The model's behavior is examined in depth, and its application is explored in
relation to yeast data, providing a potential link between the proposed
model and real-world biological systems.

In the field of speech synthesis, non-autoregressive mel-spectrogram prediction has gained significant attention due to its potential for fast and efficient speech production. Despite this promise, however, high-quality speech production using non-autoregressive models has been challenging to achieve. The reason behind this challenge is the limited ability of these models to capture long-range time-to-time dynamics, which is essential for producing high-quality speech. A recent breakthrough in this field has been made by a team of researchers who introduced a new type of non-autoregressive model that utilizes self-attention across multiple time periods to improve the prediction of speech dynamics. The model, known as Full-Attention Transformer, has demonstrated a substantial improvement in speech quality, with a significant 1.1% increase in MOS scores compared to other non-autoregressive models. Furthermore, the model's ability to predict long-range time-to-time dynamics has been confirmed by an improvement of 0.7% in MOS scores. Additionally, the model's ability to perform multi-branch prediction has been shown to enhance speech production even further.

The ternary alloy $\mathrm{Ge}_{2}\mathrm{Sb}_{2} \mathrm{Te}_5$ was investigated through cross-sectional high-resolution transmission electron microscopy and first-principles calculations. The findings revealed a unique phase, comprising alternating $\mathrm{Ge}_4\mathrm{Te}_6$ and $\mathrm{Sb}_4\mathrm{Te}_4$ clusters within a disordered $\mathrm{Ge}_2\mathrm{Te}_2$ matrix. This structure was attributed to a specific phase segregation mechanism, involving the localized Te atoms. The research confirmed that $\mathrm{Sb}_4\mathrm{Te}_4$ clusters are responsible for the material's enhanced electrical conductivity and increased optical transmittance in the amorphous phase, contrasting previous assumptions.

We develop a highly controllable model of a spin-orbital system, where it exhibits a wide range of topological insulator phases with fractional particle dynamics in 3+1 dimensions, resulting from the interplay of spin and orbital interactions. By mapping out its phase diagram, we demonstrate how these phases transition as we adjust two parameters, where we confirm the existence of a new type of fractional insulator phase with both chiral fermions and a specific set of fermion-like modes. Furthermore, we identify a previously unknown phase of the chiral fermion model emerging from the insulator system. Our research provides insights into the physics behind particle dynamics in topological insulators.

The thermal impact of gaps in protoplanetary discs is examined through the lens of thermal inversion, a phenomenon where the midplane temperature increases with altitude due to a positive temperature gradient between the midplane and atmosphere. Research has shown that thermal inversions may facilitate the formation of large gaps in discs, and could even lead to the emergence of vortices that facilitate planetesimal formation. In our study, we investigate the thermal structure of disc gaps using a disc hydrostatic model that incorporates thermal and viscous heating and cooling processes, focusing on a disc with a single gap induced by a massive planet. We find that the temperature profile around the gap supports thermal inversions, and the inversions persist for a range of disc parameters. The thermal inversion causes the midplane temperature to increase with depth, and the inversions are more pronounced for larger gap openings. This setup facilitates the formation of vortices and is consistent with the observations of ALMA's thermal inversions in the disc around TW Hya.

Utilizing large amounts of labeled data is a common approach for achieving high performance in many machine learning tasks. However, collecting high-quality data for reinforcement learning can be challenging, especially when dealing with complex environments where state variables are numerous. To address this issue, we have developed a data augmentation framework that can reduce the required amount of data for training. Our method involves randomly modifying past observation states and actions, then evaluating the feasibility of the resulting augmented states. If deemed viable, the augmented states are incorporated into the training process. We have implemented this framework using a set of predefined rules based on expert knowledge, and evaluated their effectiveness in the context of the Atari game Breakout. The results demonstrate the potential of our approach in significantly reducing the need for labeled data.

Approximately 300 million Arab speakers worldwide utilize Arabic as their official language. Although modern standard Arabic is taught in schools, dialect variations are frequently used at home. The widespread use of Arabic presents a unique challenge in developing language technologies, given the scarcity of modern standard Arabic resources and the prevalence of dialect usage. This study focuses on Arabic dialect identification, utilizing Twitter data to construct a supervised classification model. The model is trained on the ARABIC DIA dialect corpus and tested on a separate test set consisting of dialects from different regions. The proposed approach achieves an impressive 86% accuracy, even when dealing with unseen dialects.

The Strip Packing problem, specifically its variant Guillotine Strip Packing, has garnered significant research focus, with the latter being NP-hard. In this investigation, we introduce a novel, exact algorithm for solving the Guillotine Strip Packing problem, based on constraint programming and its underlying principles. To facilitate this, we define a model that accurately represents the problem, then construct an optimized solver that leverages these principles to efficiently find solutions. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we test it on benchmark datasets commonly employed in related research, comparing performance with an existing exact solver. The results indicate our method achieves superior runtime efficiency compared to the rival algorithm and, notably, consistently obtains optimal solutions when others fall short.

We have developed a novel approach to accurately infer galaxy cluster properties from simulated Compton-y maps by employing deep generative modeling techniques. By leveraging this method, we are able to generate high-fidelity mass maps that closely resemble observed data from the Planck and South Pole Telescope at a resolution of 3000 pixels. By training a neural network to project the simulated maps onto a lower-dimensional space and then reversing this process to produce a more accurate representation of the data, we are able to identify cluster mass peaks with greater precision. By using this approach to identify peaks in the data and then applying a halo model to estimate the cluster masses, we are able to achieve a high degree of accuracy with a root-mean-square error of approximately 10%. Furthermore, we find that our method provides a more accurate representation of the data than traditional methods such as the Wiener filter or halo-based approaches, and is less susceptible to noise and contamination. This breakthrough has significant implications for the field of cosmology, where we anticipate that our method will enable the creation of highly accurate simulations and data analysis pipelines that can be used to further our understanding of the universe and the properties of galaxy clusters.

This paper introduces an approach to integrating online tokenization techniques into NLP models that utilize topic modeling. By identifying word and topic combinations, it can be more effective in languages lacking clear word boundaries. A proposed method using Pearson's chi-squared test and t-statistics is presented and applied to Arabic, showing its performance in a topic modeling context, where existing approaches often struggle. Additionally, the method's ability to adjust for topic-level variability is explored.

In the field of machine learning, a significant issue exists in class imbalance, which affects the performance of classifiers when dealing with uneven distributions of data in various classes. This problem is particularly prevalent in identifying pulsar candidates. As a result of this class imbalance, the classification accuracy of these models is compromised, further exacerbated by the high noise levels inherent in the data. To mitigate this issue, a long-standing solution has been to resample the data, however, existing techniques often fail to yield satisfactory results. To address this, a novel method is proposed, which involves merging minority class samples with their corresponding majority class data while retaining the features essential for identifying pulsars. This method, which is referred to as the majority class augmentation, is demonstrated to significantly enhance the classification accuracy of these models.

For a Fell bundle over a discrete group, its full crossed product $C^*$-algebra is isomorphic to the reduced crossed product $C^*$-algebra. In this paper, the authors investigate the conditions under which the full crossed product $C^*$-algebras of such bundles have specific spectral and amenability properties. These conditions involve the bounded approximate identity of a particular subalgebra in the bundle's weighted bundle $C^*_\alpha(G)$. Amenability of the bundle is established if and only if this bounded approximate identity exists. Furthermore, the authors introduce a weaker concept of weak spectral and amenability for crossed products, and show that the bundle's $C^*$-algebra has these properties if and only if the associated crossed product $C^*$-algebra does. These findings are applied to a collection of previously studied examples, including those of certain semigroup crossed products and quantum groups.

We offer a novel, straightforward, and mathematically precise method for calculating the expressions of prolate spheroidal wave functions. These expressions are widely utilized in numerous scientific and engineering disciplines. Our proposed approach simplifies the calculation process, allowing researchers to obtain PSWF expressions for any value of the order'm', regardless of its magnitude. We demonstrate the efficacy of our algorithm through a comparison with established PSWF expressions available in existing literature.

A new strategy for crystal structure analysis has been developed, leveraging the score function concept. This strategy involves using the score function to drive a denoising process that reconstructs the true distribution of a crystal structure from noisy observations, likely due to experimental errors. The approach is flexible and can incorporate various types of information into the denoising algorithm. The method was tested using data from a rare-earth metal, Ho, and compared to a more traditional approach involving the score function with additional structural constraints. The results show that the denoising method outperforms the conventional approach in certain aspects, such as capturing the total scattering pattern and the real space correlation function.

A novel methodology, the Lagrangian approach, is employed to analyze ocean dynamics and track ocean flow pathways. By integrating the surface drifters dataset over a period, we can generate velocity profiles, model ocean circulation patterns, and track the movement of ocean flows. This study utilizes the "Stokes Drifter" dataset to create a trajectory dataset, covering an area from 2015 to 2021, and further generates a velocity field. This velocity field enables the estimation of ocean flow pathways, ultimately enabling the assessment of ocean flow patterns within the study region.

We've developed a novel approach to studying the formation of glasses. This approach is grounded in a thermodynamic scaling principle that applies to various structural properties, such as the intermediate scattering function, relaxation times, and configurational entropy density. Notably, our method has proven to be more robust than existing methods based on dynamic fluctuations. By focusing on configurational entropy density, we can isolate the effects of thermal fluctuations from those resulting from the disorder inherent in the glassy state. Through scaling analysis, we've found that the non-randomness of the glass near its transition follows a thermal pattern rather than one tied to the disorder itself.

This paper focuses on creating a new integrable discrete model from a given integrable continuous model using a specific transformation method. The paper initially discusses the basic requirements for deriving a discrete version of an integrable partial differential equation and provides an example by using the Gromov norm transform to develop a new integrable discrete model for the modified Camassa-Holm equation, with a detailed focus on analyzing its solitonic solutions.

The relationship between spin contextuality and the wave-particle duality of spin has been examined in this study.  An investigation into the nature of spin based on its particle-like and wave-like properties was conducted.  A comprehensive analysis revealed that spin particle-like properties are described by the wave function, whereas its wave-like attributes originate from the Fourier transform of the wave function.  Drawing parallels with the experiment by Aerts and Belaventu, our research proposes a spin model incorporating two states.  A crucial aspect of our model involves a hidden variable representing spin contextuality, enabling the derivation of the experiment's results without invoking wave-particle duality.  A detailed discussion of the experiment's outcomes, along with non-relativistic quantum mechanics principles, is presented, thereby providing a spin model grounded in Aerts and Belaventu's framework that does not rely on wave-particle duality.

We have conducted a detailed examination of the evolution of various mass binary systems incorporating a neutron star or black hole, focusing on the impact of gravitational interactions on the rotation dynamics of the compact objects. Our analysis, based on numerical relativity simulations, explores the evolution of these binary systems until the point at which the two components merge together. We have also considered both scenarios of spin alignment and misalignment, with the latter involving scenarios where neutron stars exhibit primordial spins. Our study demonstrates that gravitational interactions can effectively transfer angular momentum from one compact object to another, influencing the evolution of the neutron star's spin. Our numerical models reveal a clear pattern in which the neutron star's spin magnitude increases as the binary system evolves. Our results suggest that gravitational interactions can efficiently spin-up neutron stars, reaching speeds of up to 50-100% of the break-up limit, even in binary systems with black holes that are not rotating rapidly. Our study's findings are expected to shed new light on the production of millisecond pulsars, particularly those that are formed through binary evolution processes.

This work presents the "You Only Look Once" (YOLO) object detection method in detail. YOLO is a real-time object detection system, capable of processing images from multiple cameras simultaneously. In contrast to traditional object detection pipelines, YOLO operates directly on the processed image pixels without relying on region proposals. This article provides an in-depth explanation of YOLO's underlying components and reasoning, while also highlighting its key advancements. Furthermore, this research evaluates the performance of YOLO in a critical application - detecting vehicles based on license plates. Our findings demonstrate YOLO's effectiveness in identifying vehicles carrying suspicious cargo, yielding average precision and recall metrics of 0.75 and 0.71, respectively, when subjected to moderate occlusion levels.

The original Minho Quotation Database serves as a source of inspiration for investigating the impact of quotation-based information extraction on various tasks, including text classification and information retrieval. It has been updated to address issues with job titles and affiliations that were incorrectly stated in the original database. A comprehensive quality control process has ensured high accuracy in the collection. Notably, the database has been made accessible to the public under open-source licenses, utilizing GitHub for version control. Furthermore, it has been modified to facilitate the handling of quote normalization, enabling researchers to easily experiment with distinct normalization methods. A sample SQL query has been included for convenience. It is hoped that this database will foster research in the areas of information extraction, identification, and linking, as well as classification and retrieval tasks.

Decision trees and their ensembles have proven to be effective in supervised machine learning due to their strong performance and interpretability. However, their ability to handle complex data remains a challenge. This issue can be addressed by utilizing neural networks, which can effectively model various types of data. This paper introduces DeepTree, an innovative method that combines the benefits of decision trees and neural networks by integrating them into a single model. DeepTree employs a new approach to learn tree ensembles that better capture data relationships, which are encoded using a neural network. This novel strategy is integrated into a two-stage training process, where the first stage involves learning tree ensembles and the second stage involves learning a neural network classifier that combines the encoded relationships. Experimental results demonstrate that DeepTree outperforms current state-of-the-art methods across multiple benchmark datasets.

The widespread adoption of machine learning models has led to significant issues in maintaining their integrity. This paper delves into how a model's ecosystem can influence its suitability for a particular application and how poor management can compromise its functionality. Ecosystem management is a pressing concern, yet one that has been largely overlooked in the machine learning community. We investigate the impact of four common ecosystem factors - the presence of alternative models, models with improved performance, models with compromised functionality, and the influence of prominent models - on machine learning model performance. Our research reveals that these factors can have a profound effect, often resulting in decreased accuracy, and highlights the need for further study into the potential effects of ecosystem interactions on machine learning models.

In real-world applications, data can be challenging to categorize due to the emergence of novel classes and concept drifts. These phenomena necessitate the development of adaptive data classification methods. This paper focuses on a specific issue - identifying and automatically classifying rare data subclasses that arise from concept drifts within a continuous data stream. A novel approach, the Discriminative Subclass Discovery (DSCD) algorithm, has been proposed to achieve this goal. It utilizes a discriminative method to discover subclasses and applies multi-class SVMs to classify each subclass individually. To mitigate concept drifts, the DSCD algorithm employs adaptive learning strategies that leverage the performance of past data from different subclasses to update the model. Experimental results demonstrate that DSCD outperforms existing state-of-the-art class discovery techniques in terms of discovering subclasses and maintaining satisfactory classification performance.

Ptychography has become a leading method in materials science and biophysics due to its superior ability to capture detailed images of highly scattering samples, particularly with X-ray and electron beams.  However, this method's success hinges on accurately positioning a focused beam at multiple points, which can be challenging with electron beams due to their low beam current and difficulty maintaining alignment.  Our research has successfully advanced ptychography by developing a high-speed, high-resolution technique that utilizes a nanoscale electron probe at 80 As/frame with the EPW microscope, allowing us to scan at rates of up to 50 frames per second at 0.5 nm resolution.  Our results also demonstrate that by incorporating machine learning into our beam calibration process, we can significantly accelerate our scans and surpass the capabilities of traditional methods.

We introduce a gauge-invariant framework to compute the scaled cumulant-generating function, which measures fluctuations in a system's energy, entropy, and entropy production during a nonequilibrium process. Within our formalism, a standard classical observable can be transformed into a gauge-invariant observable, enabling the determination of correlation functions through path integrals and the subsequent extraction of associated cumulants. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, it is applied to a simple model: a single Brownian particle experiencing an asymmetric potential.

Artificial neural networks face a significant challenge when it comes to learning data patterns, but reservoir computing offers a more efficient alternative, allowing nodes to selectively filter input data for meaningful patterns. This approach, however, requires careful selection of the computational nodes, or "reservoir", which must be diverse and representative of the input data. In this study, we investigate the effects of network architecture on reservoir computing performance using a variety of inputs, including binary, categorical, control signals, and natural images. Our findings reveal that a robust reservoir computation is insensitive to the time series length and input type, and instead, it depends on the design of the reservoir. Specifically, we found that a sparse and modular reservoir outperforms other designs, and this effect can be attributed to the increased diversity of state vectors and the reduced correlations between them. This research demonstrates the potential of using network properties to improve machine learning, and it may also provide insights into the design of artificial neural networks.

We investigate the dynamics of Efimov states in a three-boson system following an abrupt change in interaction strength. Utilizing exact numerical results, we find that the system's short-term behavior is characterized by a dominant effect. By developing an effective model that accounts for the system's intermediate energy states, we accurately simulate and explain various aspects of the system's dynamics. Our analysis reveals that the system's long-term behavior is influenced by Efimov states and exhibits unique properties such as oscillations, colorless features, and spatial correlations, primarily driven by three-boson effects.

This study focuses on quantum machine learning techniques utilizing quantum kernel methods, particularly the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) and its implications for quantum machine learning. By examining the current state of QAOA, researchers are able to derive novel, optimized quantum kernels, and demonstrate their potential through in-depth analysis of low-rankness and positive-definiteness. These methods are further demonstrated by achieving state-of-the-art results in classification tasks on quantum machine learning datasets, while also showcasing the potential of QAOA on existing benchmark datasets.

We introduce a new method, rooted in Green's identities, to efficiently compute point particle potentials within numerical lattice QCD simulations. By leveraging Green's first and third identities, the method effectively replaces the summation over lattice sites with a convolution of two-point correlation functions. Our analysis indicates that the proposed approach retains the same computational complexity as standard summation methods, is free from numerical inaccuracies, and offers significant potential for performance enhancement depending on the chosen kernel function.
